source.title: Random Orthogonal Additive Filters: A Solution to the Vanishing/Exploding Gradient of Deep Neural Networks

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figure labels and mathematical symbols are garbled, but the text is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own training experiments on very deep networks, but uses regression and sequence-learning tasks rather than the classification-error measurements named in the versions.
record.gate_note: The experiments measure regression loss, cross-entropy, and test accuracy on double-moon, memory, adding, and psMNIST tasks. They do not report CIFAR training classification error, random-label memorization, two-layer ReLU teacher-student local minima, the named initialization comparisons, above-stability learning rates, or batch-normalization comparisons. Cited findings in Related Works and the psMNIST comparison table are not extracted as this paper's own results.
record.test_reason: The study tests a new architecture with fixed orthogonal additive transformations. It does not test initialization effects in plain networks, identity shortcuts in convolutional networks, or any other specified version. Successful training of this architecture does not establish the claims about the different architectures and interventions named in V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors propose fixed orthogonal additive transformations with depth-scaled mixing, report successful very deep FNN and long-sequence RNN training, and claim bounded Jacobian behavior under stated assumptions. The FNN theorem concerns the maximum singular value; the RNN theorem concerns all singular values. They leave global learning dynamics and the effects of orthogonal-matrix structure for further investigation.
record.recipe_differences: The proposed roaFNN and roaRNN architectures add fixed random semi-orthogonal or orthogonal matrices to nonlinear activations; experiments use regression and sequence tasks rather than the claim versions' classification or optimization measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports task-dependent optimal rho values; its identity-matrix ablation performs worse than random orthogonal matrices on the tested tasks, and the eyeRNN adding-task comparison uses tanh while the other two tasks use ReLU.

fits_no_version.finding: A shallow vanilla FNN solves double-moon regression while a similarly parameterized 50-layer vanilla FNN fails; 50-layer and 50,000-layer roaFNNs train successfully.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fixed random orthogonal additive transformations enable very deep multilayer perceptrons to train on double-moon regression.

fits_no_version.finding: roaRNN learns the tested copying-memory and adding tasks at long sequence lengths, although longer copying-memory training sometimes becomes unstable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Orthogonal additive recurrent architectures can learn long-term dependencies on these synthetic tasks, with task-dependent settings and some training instability.

fits_no_version.finding: All three tested roaRNN sizes exceed 97% psMNIST test accuracy after 10 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested roaRNN configurations rapidly attain high psMNIST test accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Section IV-D reports better performance with fixed random orthogonal transformations than with identity transformations on three recurrent tasks, despite Jacobian bounds applying to both. Learning rates differ between variants.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The structure of a fixed orthogonal additive transformation affects recurrent learning performance beyond the shared Jacobian bounds.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
record.problems: The double-moon and sequence-task curves are figure-only in the supplied text, with no numeric curve values. Copying-memory and adding-problem plots report the best results out of five trials, rather than an aggregate across trials. The paper itself notes that experiments are not fully comparable across cited psMNIST models because training methods and permutations differ, and that global learning dynamics were not theoretically investigated.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible claim-version results were reported. The psMNIST table's other architectures are cited literature results, not this paper's own results.

untested.parts: CIFAR convolutional-network training classification error, including random or corrupted labels and model-size or training-recipe effects.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student spurious minima and the effect of extra student neurons.
Depth degradation in plain convolutional networks, prevention by identity shortcuts, special initialization of plain tanh networks, and Fixup training.
Effects of initialization on plain-network training speed and trainable depth, including matched-variance Gaussian versus orthogonal weights and orthogonal convolution kernels.
Recovery above the initial stability threshold, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence relative to measured thresholds.
Batch-normalization effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and comparable training using Fixup without normalization.

record.verdict_notes: The paper discusses and cites several original sources, but its architecture experiments do not test their specified claims. Absence of normalization, clipping, or special initialization in a successful roaFNN run supplies no controlled comparison for V4 or V6. No eligible claim-version results require additional rows.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training classification error, corrupted or random labels, and effects of model size, early stopping, or regularization.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student local minima and student-width comparisons.
Plain versus identity-shortcut batch-normalized convolutional classification networks, special initialization of plain tanh networks, and Fixup residual networks.
The experiments do not compare the named initializations or establish their effect on plain-network learning speed or trainable depth.
No learning-rate stability-threshold or sharpness measurements.
No batch-normalization comparison or Fixup comparison.
